query: For a selected high-entropy alloy whose superconducting behavior remains uncharacterized, what governs whether and how superconductivity emerges in the low-temperature test regime, and why? Propose one testable mechanistic hypothesis, a controlled comparison with the starting state, the observations expected relative to that baseline, the limits over which the hypothesis should hold, supporting prior evidence, and a clear falsification criterion.

generation.hypothesis: Reducing atomic disorder via controlled thermal annealing will enhance electron–phonon coupling in the high-entropy alloy, thereby facilitating the emergence and strengthening of superconductivity at low temperatures.
generation.material_initial_state: The as-cast high-entropy alloy exhibits a high level of quenched atomic disorder without clear superconducting behavior in the low-temperature regime.
generation.intervention: Apply a controlled annealing treatment designed to reduce atomic disorder without inducing phase segregation.
generation.conditions: Compare samples over a temperature range from ~0.1 K to 10 K, using low-temperature resistivity, magnetization, and tunneling spectroscopy measurements between as-cast and post-annealed states.
generation.structural_mediator: The degree of local atomic disorder, which mediates electron–phonon interactions, serves as the structural mediator.
generation.mechanism: By annealing, the reduction in quenched disorder decreases scattering of electrons, thereby strengthening electron–phonon coupling. This improved coupling enables the formation of Cooper pairs, leading to a clear superconducting phase with a higher transition temperature and observable superconducting gap features.
generation.predicted_outcome: Post-annealed samples are expected to exhibit a higher critical temperature (Tc) and enhanced superconducting gap signatures compared to the as-cast samples, which should either be non-superconducting or show significantly lower Tc.
generation.baseline: The baseline is the as-cast alloy state, characterized by high atomic disorder and either absent or weak superconducting signals in low-temperature measurements.
generation.boundary: The hypothesis is expected to hold for the compositionally fixed high-entropy alloy when disorder reduction is achieved without altering the overall chemical makeup or inducing secondary phases. It applies within the low-temperature range (0.1–10 K) where superconductivity is probed.
generation.uncertainty: The exact magnitude of the Tc enhancement and the quantitative relationship between the degree of disorder reduction and electron–phonon coupling improvement remain uncertain, as other compositional or microstructural factors may also influence superconductivity.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of HEA samples: one in the as-cast state and one subjected to controlled annealing to reduce disorder. Cool both sets from ~0.1 K to 10 K while performing low-temperature resistivity, magnetization, and tunneling spectroscopy measurements.
measurements: Critical temperature (Tc) determined via resistivity and magnetization curves
Spectroscopic measurement of the superconducting gap
Magnetization behavior indicative of type-II superconductivity
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the annealed samples do not show a statistically significant increase in Tc or visibly stronger superconducting gap features compared to the as-cast samples, or if their superconducting properties deteriorate, then the hypothesis is falsified.

cited_evidence.text: The superconductivity of disordered materials has been extensively studied because of an observation made on the insulator-superconductor transition or disorder-induced superconductivity. In addition, recent studies on BiS2-based layered superconductors have shown the importance of controlling the local structural disorder to improve superconducting properties. As a new category of disordered superconductors, high-entropy alloys (HEAs), which are alloys containing five or more elements with an atomic concentration between 5 and 35%,, have been extensively studied, leading to the discovery of a wide range of HEA superconductors. One of the notable features is the difference in characteristics of superconductivity among conventional metal or alloy superconductors, superconducting thin films, and HEA superconductors,. Namely, the dependence of Tc on valence electron count (VEC) for HEAs exhibits interesting trends when that was compared with those for classical alloys (metals) and amorphous alloys. High-entropy alloys (HEAs) are a new type of alloy with five or more chemical elements arranged on a pseudocrystalline lattice. A high mixing-entropy minimizes the Gibbs free-energy and facilitates their crystallization on simple lattice structures, such as body-centered cubic (bcc) structure,,,. Despite the significant amount of compositional disorder, a subset of the HEAs enters a type-II superconducting phase at cryogenic temperatures,. Their large critical fields combined with superior mechanical and thermal properties render HEA promising candidates for materials applications under extreme conditions, for the fabrication of superconducting magnets, and for superconducting devices based on HEA thin films. Ongoing materials synthesis efforts have extended the family of known superconducting HEAs and developed a phenomenological understanding of their properties,. Various analyses of the upper critical field Hc2 and heat capacity measurements as a function of temperature T support a conventional Bardeen–Cooper–Schrieffer (BCS) pairing mechanism,,, with intermediate-strong coupling. occupying_moves.technique: low-temperature resistivity and magnetization measurements on as-cast versus post-annealed samples
occupying_moves.conditions: High-entropy alloy samples cooled from room temperature to sub-Kelvin temperatures to probe superconducting onset, comparing the unmodified (as-cast) state with samples subjected to controlled annealing that reduces quenched disorder

occupying_moves.technique: systematic tuning of atomic disorder via targeted thermal annealing combined with tunneling spectroscopy and conventional low-temperature transport measurements
occupying_moves.conditions: Measurements conducted from ~0.1 K up to 10 K across a series of samples with progressively reduced disorder relative to the starting state to quantify the electron-phonon coupling threshold for superconductivity and identify its mechanistic role

chosen.technique: low-temperature resistivity, magnetization, and tunneling spectroscopy measurements
chosen.conditions: A series of high-entropy alloy samples is prepared with systematic post-synthesis annealing to tune atomic disorder. Their superconducting properties are measured from ~0.1 K to 10 K, comparing each modified sample to the unmodified as-cast baseline.
chosen.why: This approach directly tests the mechanistic hypothesis that local atomic disorder (which governs electron–phonon coupling) controls the emergence and nature of superconductivity. By controlling the microstructure through annealing and employing standard low-temperature experimental techniques, the study fills the open niche by quantifying how reduced disorder promotes superconductivity, establishing clear limits and falsification criteria based on deviations in critical temperature and spectroscopic signatures.
